newsitem.title: FRANCE: French social security deficit to overrun - paper.
newsitem.headline: French social security deficit to overrun - paper.

text.p: French daily Liberation said on Thursday that the social security deficit, a key component of France's total public deficit, could hit 42-45 billion francs this year.

The newspaper cited "several experts on the case" as saying the social security deficit could come in 12-15 billion francs higher than the 30 billion initially forecast by the previous centre-right government in its 1997 budget plans.

It said the explanation given was weak revenues rather than overspending by the social security system. "Income is not in line with the forecasts issued by the last (social security) accounts commission," it quoted one expert as saying.

This year's finances are crucial to qualifying to join the launch of European monetary union but Prime Minister Lionel Jospin says he wants a flexible reading of deficit control criteria in the Maastricht treaty rather than a strict reading of the goal of limiting deficits to three percent of GDP.

The centre-right government had acknowledged -- before the June 1 election swept Jospin's left-wing coalition to power -- that the social security deficit could hit in the region of 35 billion francs.

Government sources had also confirmed the existence of a note by the finance ministry's budget division pointing to a risk of the total public deficit coming in at 3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP).
Le Monde said in April the note also contained a "worst case scenario" where the total public deficit could hit 3.8 percent of GDP, with a social security deficit of 47 billion in 1997.

Liberation's Thursday's edition quoted one social security official as saying the overshoot could leave the new left-wing government with no choice but to extend the duration of the RDS levy designed to help repay France's welfare debt.

Jospin is due to deliver his debut parliamentary speech to the National Assembly, the lower house of parliament, from 1300 GMT onwards on Thursday and is due to formally announce a promised audit of public finances.

Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn said on Tuesday the audit would probably be ready by mid-July and that it was on the basis of this assessment that the government would judge how to proceed on economic policy.

Government spokeswoman Catherine Trautmann said on Wednesday that the cabinet had ruled out extending the National Assembly session into July, making it clear any mini-budget would have to wait until September at the earliest, after the summer recess.
Jospin is thus expected to provide limited insight in his keynote speech on concrete economic figures.
